title: OnboardX: The Ghost of Community Knowledge Shouldn’t Disappear
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 4 — Ghost in the Machine.

What I Built

When student community leaders leave, what happens to everything they learned?

There might be a handover document somewhere. Some explanations are buried in chats. Other things only exist in someone’s head: why a venue was chosen, what went wrong during a workshop, or which project the next team should continue.

As someone involved in student communities at FUTMinna, this is a problem I care about. The next team should have something useful to build on.

I built OnboardX, a local community memory and handover app. It lets you save decisions, lessons and unfinished work, ask questions about those records, and generate an editable handover draft.

My Interpretation of “Ghost in the Machine”

I approached the theme through the knowledge previous teams leave behind.

A former lead might have moved on, but their documented experience can still help the next person make a decision. OnboardX makes those records easier to find and use.

It doesn’t impersonate previous leaders. It answers from what they recorded and shows the source.

Demo

Repository: https://github.com/ufidscript/onboardx

Demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lp8-wIt36VM



The app includes a fictional sample community so people can explore it without needing private community documents.

The main journey is:

  1. Save a memory with a title, category and content.
  2. Ask a question about the archive.
  3. Read the answer alongside its supporting excerpts.
  4. Generate a handover draft, review it and export Markdown.

One question I tested was:

Why did we choose the library?

OnboardX answered that the library had reliable power and seating. Under the answer, it showed the saved “Workshop venue decision” record containing that explanation.

I also asked for the president’s phone number, which wasn’t in the records. It responded:

I couldn't find that in the saved records.

That second result matters to me. A handover tool needs to make gaps visible, because the next team might act on what it says.

How It Works

The frontend uses React and Vite, with an Express backend and a local JSON file for persistence.

Saved memories are split into smaller excerpts. When someone asks a question, lightweight keyword retrieval selects relevant excerpts and passes them to Gemma 3 1B through Ollama.

The model produces a structured JSON response. The backend checks its format and citation IDs, then resolves those IDs to the stored excerpts shown in the interface.

This helps keep references tied to actual records. It doesn’t guarantee that every generated sentence is correct, so the original text remains available for inspection.

The handover feature uses the archive to draft sections covering context, decisions, lessons, unfinished work and gaps. Users can edit the draft before exporting it.

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma

OnboardX uses Gemma 3 1B locally through Ollama to answer questions using retrieved community records and generate editable handover drafts. Gemma powers the core AI features while keeping inference on the user’s machine.

Best Use of GitHub Copilot

I used the GitHub Copilot app to build and debug OnboardX incrementally, including the React interface, Express endpoints, retrieval, citation validation and handover export. I guided the implementation and manually tested the application locally.

Why Open Innovation Matters Here

Community handover records can contain internal discussions and decisions. I wanted a version that could run with the records and model on the same machine.

Using an open-weight model through Ollama makes local inference possible. The core workflow doesn’t require a hosted AI API, and the model can be changed through configuration.

There are still setup requirements: users need to install the dependencies, Ollama and the model. Local inference also uses the laptop’s resources. But there is no per-request hosted AI charge for this setup.

For a tool intended to preserve knowledge, being able to keep and run the system yourself is part of its value.

Building It—and Learning Along the Way

I built with the GitHub Copilot app and tested the results locally.

Getting the app running took some debugging. Node wasn’t initially available in my terminal. After installing it, I ran into missing dependencies, then opened the backend address expecting to see the frontend and got Cannot GET /.

Working through those steps helped me understand the separate jobs of the React development server and the Express API.

Testing also exposed a more meaningful issue: an unanswered question could still display an unrelated retrieved record under “Sources.” That made the distinction between retrieved text and supporting evidence very clear. Finding a record does not mean it supports the answer.

The most satisfying moment was seeing a question answered with the exact saved explanation underneath it. That made the idea feel useful beyond being another chat interface.

Current Limitations

This is a local prototype with a focused scope:

  • It has no accounts or shared online workspace.
  • Keyword retrieval can miss relevant records when questions use different wording.
  • Gemma 3 1B can make mistakes.
  • Generated handovers need human review.
  • Markdown export creates a readable handover; it doesn’t automatically transfer the searchable archive to another device.

I’d like to improve retrieval and archive portability next. For this version, my priority was a working path from saving knowledge to asking about it and preparing a handover.

AI Assistance Disclosure

I used GitHub Copilot to assist with implementation and debugging, and ChatGPT to help with planning and this write-up. I directed the work and manually tested the local application. This was an AI-assisted build.

If you’ve ever taken over a student community or team, what was the one thing you wish the previous leaders had written down?

title: LOKĀNTRA: AI-Powered Multi-Agent Simulation & Swarm Intelligence Platform
summary:
Project: https://github.com/vedhanth66/Lokantra

Tagline: PREDICT the UNPREDICTABLE.

Developed LOKĀNTRA, an AI-powered simulation platform that transforms real-world documents and scenarios into interactive knowledge graphs and simulated social environments populated by AI agents.

The platform explores how different stakeholders might react to events, influence one another, and collectively shape possible outcomes. Rather than relying on a single LLM-generated prediction, it combines multi-agent simulation, graph-based knowledge retrieval, intelligent decision routing, and evidence-grounded reporting.

KEY ENGINEERING CONTRIBUTIONS AND FEATURES

  1. Knowledge Graph Engineering: Implemented dynamic ontology generation and document-to-knowledge-graph pipelines using TigerGraph and Zep Cloud.

  2. Multi-Agent AI Simulation: Integrated CAMEL-AI and OASIS to create simulated personas and model interactions across Reddit-style and Twitter-style environments.

  3. Cognitive Swarm Routing: Developed a hierarchical decision architecture combining heuristic reflex gating, LAYA System 1 decision intelligence, and LLM-based reasoning.

  4. Neuromorphic Computing Research: Explored BrainChip Akida-inspired spiking neural network reflex gating as an experimental approach to reducing unnecessary agent computations.

  5. Graph-Based Memory and Retrieval: Integrated graph-backed memory and retrieval mechanisms to provide contextual information for simulation analysis.

  6. Agent Interrogation: Enabled users to interview individual simulated agents and investigate the reasoning behind their decisions, opinions, and reactions.

  7. Autonomous Report Generation: Developed a tool-assisted ReportAgent that retrieves simulation evidence, generates structured analytical reports, supports follow-up conversations, and exports PDFs.

  8. Token-Aware Processing: Implemented representative document chunking, context management, staged generation, and decision-tier telemetry to help optimize LLM usage.

  9. Voice-Based Input: Integrated a configurable Sarvam AI Saaras speech-to-text pipeline for natural-language scenario input.

  10. Enterprise Integration Research: Incorporated viaSocket MCP configuration for external integrations and human-in-the-loop action workflows.

TECHNOLOGY STACK

Python, Flask, Vue.js 3, Vite, JavaScript, TigerGraph, Zep Cloud, GraphRAG, CAMEL-AI, OASIS, LAYA, BrainChip Akida (experimental), OpenAI-compatible LLM APIs, Sarvam AI, Supabase, D3.js, MCP, viaSocket, Docker.

CORE VISION

Move beyond static AI predictions towards interactive simulations where users can explore possible futures, investigate individual perspectives, and understand the dynamics behind emerging outcomes.

title: The Last Echo: An Offline AI That Keeps Memories Alive
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

The Last Echo – An Offline AI Memory Keeper

What if the stories of the people we love never had to disappear?

For Ghost in the Machine, I wanted to explore something beyond traditional horror. I wanted to build something that feels a little mysterious but carries a deeper human meaning.

The Last Echo is an AI-powered digital memory keeper designed to preserve the stories, memories, photographs, and personal experiences of loved ones.

Users can add memories, write personal stories, preserve meaningful conversations, and organize important moments. They can then interact with an AI assistant that retrieves relevant memories and responds using the information they have preserved.

Inspired by Día de los Muertos, the project is built around one simple idea:

Technology should not just remember information. It should help us preserve the stories that make us human.

The AI doesn't claim to bring people back or actually recreate someone's consciousness. Instead, it helps people revisit the memories and stories they've chosen to preserve.

Demo

Coming soon!

A demonstration will showcase:

  • Adding and preserving personal memories.
  • Organizing stories into a searchable memory collection.
  • Asking questions about saved memories.
  • Receiving context-aware responses from a locally running AI model.
  • Accessing the experience without an internet connection after initial setup.

Code

GitHub repository: Coming soon.

The project source code, installation instructions, architecture, and implementation details will be published here.

How I Built It

The core idea behind The Last Echo is to make open-source AI the engine of the entire experience rather than simply connecting to a commercial AI API.

Planned technology stack:

  • Ollama: Local inference and model management.
  • Llama or another suitable open-weight model: Powers the conversational memory assistant.
  • Python: Backend logic and memory processing.
  • LangChain: Helps orchestrate retrieval and language-model interactions.
  • ChromaDB: Stores and retrieves memory embeddings.
  • Sentence Transformers: Generates embeddings for semantic memory search.
  • Streamlit: Provides an interactive user interface.

The architecture follows a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) approach.

When someone saves a memory, the application converts it into an embedding and stores it locally. When a user asks a question, the system retrieves relevant memories and provides them as context to the local language model.

This helps the assistant generate responses grounded in the information the user actually provided.

The long-term goal is a completely local experience where personal memories never need to be sent to an external AI service.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

For a project dealing with personal memories, privacy isn't an optional feature. It's the foundation.

Imagine preserving your family's photographs, personal stories, and private conversations in a system that sends everything to an external AI provider.

That creates a difficult question: Who really owns those memories?

Open-source AI gives us another path.

By using open-weight models and local inference, The Last Echo can be designed to:

  • Keep personal memories on the user's own machine.
  • Work without an internet connection after downloading the required models and dependencies.
  • Allow users to choose, replace, or customize their language models.
  • Avoid depending on a single commercial AI provider.
  • Give developers control over how personal information is processed.

A closed API might make the initial development easier, but local open AI makes the project's privacy-first philosophy possible.

For me, that's the real value of open innovation: having the freedom to build technology around people's needs instead of forcing people to adapt to a service's limitations.

My Agent Session

Coming soon!

I plan to share the development process and agent session through DevRelay.

The Spirit of It

There is something haunting about forgetting.

A photograph can fade. A voice recording can get lost. A story that someone tells us today might disappear if nobody remembers to tell it again.

Día de los Muertos reminds us that remembering someone is also a way of keeping their presence in our lives.

The Last Echo explores that idea through technology.

Imagine asking:

"What was Grandpa's favorite story about his childhood?"

And receiving an answer based on a story that your family personally preserved.

It isn't the person speaking again.

It's their story finding its way back to you.

Some echoes deserve to last forever.

Prize Categories

Primary challenge entry:

  • Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge – Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

Partner categories: To be confirmed based on the final implementation and actual partner technology used.

Built with the belief that the best use of AI isn't always creating something new. Sometimes, it's helping us hold on to what matters. -->

title: Kimi K3.1 Pro Weights Drop Nov 4: Licence, Size, How to Run
summary:
On November 4, 2026, Moonshot AI is scheduled to do something no lab has done before: hand the public the complete weights of a 2.8-trillion-parameter AI model that independent testing currently ranks as the strongest open model in the world. Kimi K3.1 Pro has been live through Moonshot's apps and API since October 23, but the downloadable release — the one that lets anyone outside Moonshot run, inspect, fine-tune and redistribute the model — is still a promise with a date on it. We checked Moonshot's Hugging Face organisation while writing this article: there is no K3.1 Pro repository yet. The newest thing there is still the older Kimi K3. So this is the guide to read before the drop: what exactly is landing, the licence question that will decide what "open" really means here, the terabyte-scale hardware reality, the two controversies hanging over the release, and a checklist for the day itself. For the launch story — benchmarks, pricing and how the model performs — start with our Kimi K3.1 Pro launch guide; this article is about the weights.

What exactly is dropping on November 4

Kimi K3.1 Pro is not a new architecture. It is a heavily post-trained version of Kimi K3, the model Moonshot released in the summer: a mixture-of-experts system with 2.8 trillion total parameters, of which about 104 billion are active on any given token. It uses Moonshot's Kimi Delta Attention and Attention Residuals design, reads text, images and video in a single model, and works across a context window of one million tokens. What the extra post-training bought is measurable: on Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index, K3 scored 44; K3.1 Pro scores 55, fourth of every model the evaluator tracks and only three points behind the best closed model, Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5.

"Full model weights" is the phrase that matters. A weight file is the trained model itself — the numbers that encode everything it learned. With the weights, the model stops being a service you rent from Moonshot and becomes a file you possess: you can run it on hardware you control, fine-tune it on your own data, inspect its behaviour without an API in between, and keep it forever even if Moonshot changes its prices, its terms, or its mind. That is why a weights release is a different event from an API launch, and why the October 23 launch, impressive as it was, is only half the story.

Two things about the drop are still unknown, and both matter. First, Moonshot has not said whether the faster K3.1 Pro Highspeed variant is part of the weights release or stays a hosted-only product. Second — and this is the big one — Moonshot has not named the licence. More on that below, because there is a very good precedent to read in the meantime.

Here is what the family looks like side by side. The K3 column is verified from the actual Hugging Face repository; the K3.1 Pro column is what is known or reasonably expected before November 4, and every expectation is labelled as one.

Kimi K3 (already out) Kimi K3.1 Pro (weights due Nov 4)
Total / active parameters 2.8 trillion / ~104 billion 2.8 trillion / ~104 billion (same base)
Context window 1 million tokens 1 million tokens
Input Text, images, video Text, images, video
Weight format MXFP4 weights, MXFP8 activations Not yet published; MXFP4 expected
Download size on Hugging Face 1.56 TB across 96 files Not yet published; similar scale expected
Licence Kimi K3 License (custom) Not yet announced
Serving vLLM and SGLang, official recipes Not yet published; same stacks expected
API price $3 / $15 per million tokens $2 / $10 per million tokens

The licence question — and what K3's licence actually says

Everything about this release hinges on a document that does not exist yet. "Open weights" tells you the file is downloadable; it says nothing about what you are allowed to do with it. That is the licence's job, and Moonshot's announcement named none. The honest position today is: unknown, decided on November 4.

But we are not guessing in the dark, because Kimi K3 shipped under a licence Moonshot wrote for exactly this model family, and you can read it in full in the Kimi K3 repository on Hugging Face. It is a short, unusually readable document, and if K3.1 Pro follows the same pattern — which is an expectation, not a fact — this is what "open" will mean in practice.

The Kimi K3 License starts like the famous MIT licence: permission to use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense and sell the software — explicitly including the weights, the code and the right to fine-tune and build derivative works — free of charge. For researchers, hobbyists, and the overwhelming majority of companies, that is the whole story: download it and build.

Then come two conditions aimed at the very top of the market. The first is the "Model as a Service" clause. If you or your affiliates run a business that gives third parties API-style access to model inference or fine-tuning — where those third parties meaningfully control inputs, parameters or training data — and that business's aggregate revenue exceeds 20 million US dollars over any consecutive twelve months, you must sign a separate agreement with Moonshot before using the model commercially. Note what the clause deliberately does not cover: products that merely embed the model inside specific features, and simple relays of requests to models hosted by others. The second condition is a branding rule: if the model powers a commercial product with more than 100 million monthly active users, or more than 20 million dollars in monthly revenue, the name "Kimi K3" must be prominently displayed in that product's interface.

A final carve-out softens both conditions: they do not apply to purely internal use — anything that never exposes the model, its outputs or its capabilities to third parties — nor to use through Moonshot's own products and certified inference partners. And the licence closes with the standard "as is" disclaimer and a contact address for licensing questions.

So when the K3.1 Pro licence appears, the checklist is short and specific. Is it the same Kimi K3 License with the name swapped, or a new document? Is the Model-as-a-Service revenue threshold still 20 million dollars? Does the branding rule survive? Has anything been added — an acceptable-use list, a geographic restriction, a research-only tier? Five minutes of reading on November 4 will answer all of it, and until those five minutes happen, any article that tells you what you may do with these weights — including confident claims that they are "fully open" or "not really open" — is getting ahead of the document.

One and a half terabytes: the hardware reality

The second reality check is physical. The Kimi K3 weights on Hugging Face occupy 1.56 terabytes, spread across 96 files, in MXFP4 format — a compact 4-bit representation that Moonshot bakes in during training rather than squeezing down afterwards. K3.1 Pro is the same architecture at the same parameter count, so a similar footprint is the reasonable expectation. To put 1.56 terabytes in perspective: it is roughly twenty-five times the size of a typical 70-billion-parameter model download, and it will not fit on the drive of most workstations, let alone in the memory of a gaming GPU.

Running it is a data-centre conversation, and the arithmetic is not complicated. The weights alone need about 1.6 terabytes of fast memory before you have processed a single token; on top of that sits the key-value cache for that million-token context, which grows with every conversation you serve. A top-end data-centre GPU carries around 141 to 192 gigabytes of high-bandwidth memory. title: Graveyard: a funeral for dead code, with a checker that keeps the AI honest
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Graveyard is a funeral for dead code. Every repo has a graveyard: files deleted with a commit message like "fix stuff" and never thought about again. For the Ghost in the Machine theme, I wanted to dig them up and give each one a tombstone.

A small Node script reads a git repo's history (read-only) and exports every deleted file as JSON. The page then draws a candlelit cemetery with one tombstone per file: born, died, an epitaph, and the real commit message that killed it. The idea is that a local open-weight model, Gemma 3 4B through Ollama, writes the epitaph and the cause of death.

My reading of the theme: the ghost in the machine is the AI inventing a backstory for something that can't correct it. So the part I spent the most time on is a checker that stops the model from making things up.

  • Dates, file names and commit hashes come from the repo, never from the model.
  • The "cause of death" has to share most of its key words with the real commit message, or it is replaced with "Cause of death unknown" and marked "Unverified claim removed".
  • An epitaph that mentions a number, date or hash that isn't in the data is replaced with a plain one.

Demo

Live demo (fake data, canned text, no model): https://p44-code.github.io/graveyard/

In the demo, one tombstone has a cause of death I planted on purpose. Its real commit message is just "fix stuff", but the canned answer talks about memory leaks. The checker catches it, shows "Cause of death unknown", and prints the original commit message underneath.

An important note: the online demo uses canned text, not model output. GitHub Pages can't run Ollama on your computer, so the live demo only shows the page and the checker.

"Theme: Ghost in the Machine — Memorializing the code we wrote, loved, refactored, and purged."

Graveyard is a solemn, client-side digital cemetery for retired source code files. It transforms Git deletion logs into atmospheric, Gothic terminal tombstones commemorating deprecated shims, abandoned hacks, and forgotten features.

Built for open-source AI challenges with a strict security-first architecture:

title: Addendum R2: La tasa que faltaba, medida sobre las dos clases que faltaban
summary:
Addendum R2 — la tasa que faltaba, medida sobre las dos clases que faltaban

Este artículo sustituye como lectura al anterior —«Addendum: corregí mi propio instrumento y el número bajó de
807 a 612»: https://dev.to/alexisromtz7/addendum-corregi-mi-propio-instrumento-y-el-numero-bajo-de-807-a-612-5172—
cuyo cuerpo se publicó sin el Markdown con que fue escrito: la plataforma guardó el texto y descartó la sintaxis.
El contenido es el mismo; la forma no. Se republica para que se pueda leer lo que se midió. El original sigue vivo y
sin editar, como registro de lo que el entorno de publicación hizo con él (§9).

Este documento no reescribe el anterior. El addendum publicado con RC 2 y RC 4
(ADDENDUM_ARTICULO_20261030.md, blob 723dda49, vivo en Dev.to) queda intacto byte a byte, porque un acto
público no se corrige por edición: se corrige por adenda. Lo que sigue sustituye solo su sección «La tasa que
faltaba», y solo en la parte que dejó abierta.

Huella de esta revisión: HUELLA-ADDENDUM-R2-TPR-RC1-RC5-20261030. Se declara como texto en código y no como
comentario HTML por la razón medida en §9.

1. Lo que quedaba abierto, dicho con la cifra al lado

El addendum anterior cerró la tasa de RC 2 y RC 4: 33 casos, 100% formal, 15.2% sustantiva. Y declaró su
propio residuo en la misma página: RC 1 (60) y RC 5 (308) seguían sin tasa.

Eso significa que 368 de las 612 observaciones publicadas — el 60,1% del numerador — no tenían veredicto. Un
cliente que preguntara «¿cuál es tu tasa de falsos positivos?» recibía una respuesta que valía para 33 casos y se
presentaba como si valiera para 612. Esa era la debilidad, y no estaba escondida: estaba escrita.

Ya no está abierta.

2. La medición

Misma disciplina que la vez anterior, y en el mismo orden: primero la predicción, después la lectura.

Se escribió un pre-registro (preregistro_tpr_rc1_rc5_20261030.json, 129 líneas, blob 05eaead8) con las clases
sustantivas, el sesgo declarado y cinco falsadores, antes de abrir un solo run: o un solo uses:. Después se
re-descargaron los 163 archivos de workflow del lote por blob SHA desde la API de GitHub y se verificó su
sha256 contra el manifiesto: 163/163 idénticos, 0 fallos. El motor reprodujo el reparto exacto:
RC 1 60 · RC 2 30 · RC 4 3 · RC 5 308.

clase lectura resultado
RC 5 REF_MUTABLE ¿el uses: citado existe en el crudo y su ref es realmente flotante? 308/308, 0 falsos positivos
RC 1 AUTORIDAD_CONTAMINADA ¿el job tiene escritura y ejecuta código en la misma línea citada? 60/60, 0 falsos positivos
Control negativo RC 5 de 1321 uses:, 1013 están fijados a SHA de 40: ¿cuántos marca el motor? 0 de 1013
Control negativo RC 1 164 jobs ejecutan código de terceros sin scope de escritura: ¿cuántos marca? 0 de 164

Los dos controles negativos son la parte que importa. Un motor que marcara todo habría dado 1321 en lugar de 308, y
174 en lugar de 60. No los da: discrimina en los dos sentidos de la conjunción.

3. La tasa sustantiva: aquí es donde el número se encoge

Formal 100% no es la cifra que se puede vender, y el addendum anterior ya lo dijo para RC 2. Para RC 1 y RC 5
el efecto es mayor, porque estas dos clases se miden por ocurrencia y no por riesgo.

RC 5 — 308 ocurrencias no son 308 riesgos: son 31

El barrido de RC 5 no deduplica. Una misma acción repetida en veinte jobs produce veinte hallazgos. En los 163
archivos hay 1321 valores uses:, de los cuales 308 son flotantes… y esos 308 son solo 31 referencias
distintas. Publicar 308 sin decirlo sería inflar el numerador por la puerta de atrás.

clase ocurrencias distintas qué es
Primera parte (actions/*) 239 17 etiqueta móvil de GitHub sobre código de GitHub. Patrón documentado
Tercero, etiqueta flotante 42 5 pnpm/action-setup@v6, dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable, oven-sh/setup-bun@v2, rust-lang/crates-io-auth-action@v1, vercel/next.js/.github/actions/pr-auto-label@canary
Workflow reutilizable flotante 10 6 un workflow entero de otro repo ejecutado con el token de este
Placeholder sin sustituir 17 3 ver §4 — clase que la predicción no tenía
Imagen docker sin digest 0 0 predije 8; no hay una sola en los 10 repos

La superficie de terceros real: 52 ocurrencias y 11 referencias distintas — el 16,9% de las ocurrencias y el
35,5% de las distintas. Las otras 256 se reparten en 239 actions/*, que para un cliente es ruido (el control del
ref lo tiene GitHub, no el atacante que el cliente teme), y 17 placeholders que no resuelven y que van contados como
clase propia en §4, no como terceros.

Corrección con cadena (HUELLA-ADDENDUM-R2-CORRECCION-PORCENTAJE-TERCEROS-20261030). La primera versión de este
párrafo, escrita horas antes y nunca publicada, decía 22,4% y «las otras 239». Ese porcentaje es correcto para 69
ocurrencias, no para 52: la frase había sumado al numerador las 17 de R7, que son rutas $/.github/… del propio
repositorio del cliente y por tanto no son código de un tercero. La tabla de arriba nunca dijo 69; decía 42 + 10.
El número de la prosa y el de su propia tabla no medían lo mismo, y nada los comparaba. Se conserva el literal
equivocado a la vista porque un addendum que corrige cifras no puede editarse en silencio —esa es la misma regla que
lo hizo nacer—. La corrección viaja con el censo:
INVESTIGACION/evidencia/censo_tpr_rc1_rc5_20261030.json, campo superficie_de_terceros.correccion_con_cadena.

RC 1 — 60 hallazgos, 10 sostienen el nombre del código

RC 1 se llama AUTORIDAD_CONTAMINADA. La conjunción que mide —escritura y ejecución en el mismo job— es
correcta y da 60/60 formal. Pero solo una parte de esas 60 líneas ejerce o entrega la autoridad:

clase n qué es
A1 — escritura remota ejercida 9 gh run cancel, gh pr comment, gh api --method POST: el token es el instrumento de esa misma línea
A2 — descarga a ejecución 1 `curl https://rustwasm.github.io/…/init.sh -sSf \
A3 — hereda terceros 28 {% raw %}pnpm install, cargo build, npx -y firebase-tools@15.15.0, cargo binstall, gh corriendo con el token disponible
A4 — mutación local 5 git config sin push: la autoridad está declarada y no se ejerce
A5 — código del propio repo 11 pnpm run build, node scripts/…: el que ve el token es el dueño del repo
A7 — lexema sin ejecución 6 ver §4

Autoridad ejercida o entregada: 10 de 60 (16,7%). Ese es el número que la palabra «contaminada» puede defender.

4. Las dos clases que la predicción no tenía

En dos días consecutivos, el mismo patrón: la taxonomía se queda corta y la clase nueva aparece en el mismo lugar
donde el motor lee bien. Ayer fue NO_SUMIDERO (16 de 33). Hoy son dos, y las dos se declaran en vez de encajarse.

R7 — placeholder sin sustituir: 17 ocurrencias, 3 literales, 3 repositorios y 6 archivos. Los bytes crudos
contienen referencias locales escritas con el placeholder de plantilla de GitHub ($/…) que nunca se sustituyó:
$/.github/actions/setup 5 veces, todas en sveltejs/svelte ci.yml; $/.github/actions/issues-helper
11 veces en vitejs/vite —6 en bot.yml, 3 en issue-labeled.yml, 1 en issue-close-require.yml, 1 en
lock-closed-issues.yml—; y $/.github/workflows/notify-resolved-issues.yml 1 vez en nuxt/nuxt release.yml.
Los bytes son genuinos del origen: el git hash-object de los seis archivos coincide uno por uno con el blob_sha
que declara el manifiesto, así que no es un artefacto de la descarga. Su severidad queda NO_MEDIDO, por la misma
razón que NO_SUMIDERO: 0 si se lee que un uses que no resuelve no custodia nada, y «el hallazgo más fuerte» si se
lee que el archivo declara una intención que no ejecuta y quien lo audite creerá que está fijado. Resolverlo exige
saber si el repo genera ese archivo o lo commitea tal cual, y el archivo no lo dice.

Corrección con cadena (HUELLA-ADDENDUM-R2-R7-POR-ARCHIVO-20261030). La versión anterior de este párrafo, escrita
horas antes y nunca publicada, nombraba facebook/react como uno de los repositorios con placeholders. Medido sobre
los 163 workflows ya verificados por sha256: facebook/react tiene 26 workflows y cero ocurrencias, y los 17
están en svelte (5), vite (11) y nuxt (1). El conteo nunca cambió —17 ocurrencias, 3 literales—; la atribución
sí. Es el tercer caso del mismo defecto en la jornada: un campo estructurado correcto al lado de una frase que no
se deriva de él, igual que el 22,4% de §5. La corrección viaja con el censo, campo
clase_no_prevista.correccion_con_cadena.

A7 — el lexema casa sin que nada se ejecute: 6 de 60. Un echo " - NPM name: …" casa con el patrón de npm.
Un yq '.allowBuilds[]=false' -i pnpm-workspace.yaml casa porque el nombre del archivo dice pnpm. No es un
defecto del motor —su dominio declarado es léxico por línea— pero sí es ruido para un cliente, y por eso se cuenta
aparte y se publica: es la forma en que un falso positivo sobrevive a la corrección del motor.

5. Cuatro defectos del lector, encontrados antes de publicar

La lección de la vez anterior se aplicó con saña: el lector también se equivoca, y cuando se equivoca declara
culpable al instrumento correcto. Un lector independiente de mesa, sin el parser del motor, encontró cuatro:

  1. permissions: {} leído como {'{}': 'write'} → RC 1 inflado de 60 a 121 (61 falsos rojos).
  2. El uses: de job contado dos veces → RC 5 inflado de 308 a 319 (11 falsos rojos).
  3. Valores de permiso entrecomillados (contents: 'read') conservando las comillas → un job real quedaba fuera: 59 de 60.
  4. run: plegado en varias líneas leído solo en la primera → una línea citada aparecía truncada.

Los cuatro eran del lector. El motor no cambió una línea: su salida formal se sostiene 368/368.

6. Predicción contra medición, sin maquillar

predicción (pre-registrada) medido veredicto
RC 5: 308 TP, 0 FP, ±4 308 / 0 cumplida
RC 1: 60 TP, 0 FP, ±6 60 / 0 cumplida
31 a 60 literales distintos, punto 45 31 cumplida al borde, por un literal
Reparto RC 5: 240 / 55 / 8 / 3 / 2 / 0 239 / 42 / 0 / 10 / 0 / 17 dirección correcta, tres desvíos
Terceros distintos: 12 ± 6 11 cumplida
A1+A2: 9 ± 6 10 cumplida

Tres desvíos que se publican porque se midieron: la imagen docker sin digest no existe en los 10 repos (predije
8), el workflow reutilizable flotante es el triple de lo predicho (3 → 10, y es la clase más fuerte de las
cuatro), y apareció una clase que no estaba en la taxonomía (R7, 17). El punto de 45 contra 31 no es un fallo de
método: es la diferencia entre estimar cuántas ocurrencias habría y contar cuántas referencias distintas hay.

7. Lo que sigue sin tasa, y por qué se dice

SC1 — 211 observaciones, y no todas son la misma cosa. No son del gate: son el recuento de sustitución y cadena
del propio arnés. Con este acto se miden 368 de 612 observaciones (60,1%) — pero ese denominador no es el de
hallazgos, y confundirlos es el defecto que este addendum ya cometió una vez con otra cifra. De las 244 sin censo,
156 son REVIEW por diseño del contrato (SC1_JOB_WRITE_SCOPE_REVIEW 153 + SC1_ROOT_READ_ALL_REVIEW 3): son
inventario, no hallazgo, y no hay tasa que asignarles porque no afirman una vulnerabilidad. 55 sí son conjunción
real (SC1_ROOT_PERMISSIONS_MISSING 36 + SC1_ROOT_WRITE_INHERITED 19). Y 33 son la clase corregida (RC 2 30

  • RC 4 3), validada por revisión de dominio con cadena, no por censo. Sobre el denominador que un CTO querría —el de las que afirman una vulnerabilidad, 456— la cobertura es 368/456 = 80,7%, y lo que falta censar son 55 casos, el 9,0% del total, no 211. Lo que se publica como 60,1% sigue siendo correcto mientras el denominador sea «observaciones»; deja de serlo en cuanto el denominador es «hallazgos».

Huella de esta revisión: HUELLA-ADDENDUM-R2-DENOMINADOR-20261030 (§MEDICIÓN CON UNIDAD, aplicado al propio
enunciado: el 60,1% no estaba mal, estaba midiendo otra población).

Y tres residuos más, declarados: RC 5 emite job: '-', así que no dice qué job consume la acción y la
severidad por job queda NO_MEDIDA; el residuo propio del motor sigue vigente (env: con secretos + ejecución de
terceros sólo cae bajo RC 1 si hay scopes de escritura); y la lectura sustantiva es de mesa, sobre el YAML, sin
ejecutar los workflows: no mide si una acción de terceros es hostil hoy, mide si el ref es fijable y si la autoridad
se ejerce.

8. La frase que sí se puede publicar

612 observaciones, de las cuales 456 afirman una vulnerabilidad. Censadas: 368 — el 80,7% de los hallazgos y el
60,1% de las observaciones. De las 244 restantes: 156 son inventario REVIEW por contrato, 55 son conjunción
real sin censar y 33 son la clase corregida, validada por revisión de dominio.
TPR formal 368/368. Control negativo: 1013 refs fijadas sin marcar y 164 jobs sin escritura sin marcar.
Sustantiva: 10 de 60 hallazgos de autoridad ejercen o entregan la credencial; 11 referencias distintas de
terceros en 308 ocurrencias de ref flotante; 17 referencias que no resuelven —5 en sveltejs/svelte ci.yml,
11 en cuatro workflows de vitejs/vite (6 de ellas en bot.yml), 1 en nuxt/nuxt release.yml—, con
severidad NO_MEDIDO.

No hay un número redondo y no lo va a haber. Lo que hay es un instrumento que se equivocó 195 veces, lo publicó, se
corrigió, midió su propia tasa, encontró cuatro defectos en su lector y los publicó también, y dejó a la vista lo
que no pudo medir. Eso es lo que un CTO puede auditar. Un «1000 vulnerabilidades» no.

9. Nota de publicación: el formato declarado y el formato ejecutado

El addendum anterior se escribió en Markdown y se publicó sin él. Medido hoy contra la API pública (GET
/api/articles/4950016, HTTP 200, published_at 2026-10-31T00:18:48Z): el body_markdown almacenado contiene
0 **, 0 comillas invertidas, 0 | y 0 ##. La pérdida no está en el render: está en la fuente.
Por eso el formato no se recupera cambiando de modo en el editor — hay que reescribir el cuerpo.

Y hay un detalle que sí es un mecanismo, no un accidente: de los dos comentarios HTML del cuerpo publicado, el que
abría línea perdió su < (!-- HUELLA-TPR-MEDIDA…, visible como texto) y el que iba en línea detrás del -->
sobrevivió intacto (

sha256 contra el manifiesto: 163/163 idénticos, 0 fallos. El motor reprodujo el reparto exacto:
RC 1 60 · RC 2 30 · RC 4 3 · RC 5 308.

clase lectura resultado
RC 5 REF_MUTABLE ¿el uses: citado existe en el crudo y su ref es realmente flotante? 308/308, 0 falsos positivos

3. La tasa sustantiva: aquí es donde el número se encoge

El barrido de RC 5 no deduplica. Una misma acción repetida en veinte jobs produce veinte hallazgos. En los 163
archivos hay 1321 valores uses:, de los cuales 308 son flotantes… y esos 308 son solo 31 referencias

INVESTIGACION/evidencia/censo_tpr_rc1_rc5_20261030.json, campo superficie_de_terceros.correccion_con_cadena.

clase n qué es

lee que el archivo declara una intención que no ejecuta y quien lo audite creerá que está fijado. Resolverlo exige

aparte y se publica: es la forma en que un falso positivo sobrevive a la corrección del motor.

5. Cuatro defectos del lector, encontrados antes de publicar

La lección de la vez anterior se aplicó con saña: el lector también se equivoca, y cuando se equivoca declara
culpable al instrumento correcto. Un lector independiente de mesa, sin el parser del motor, encontró cuatro:

  1. permissions: {} leído como {'{}': 'write'} → RC 1 inflado de 60 a 121 (61 falsos rojos).
  2. El uses: de job contado dos veces → RC 5 inflado de 308 a 319 (11 falsos rojos).
  3. Valores de permiso entrecomillados (contents: 'read') conservando las comillas → un job real quedaba fuera: 59 de 60.
  4. run: plegado en varias líneas leído solo en la primera → una línea citada aparecía truncada.

Los cuatro eran del lector. El motor no cambió una línea: su salida formal se sostiene 368/368.

6. Predicción contra medición, sin maquillar

RC 5: 308 TP, 0 FP, ±4 308 / 0 cumplida
RC 1: 60 TP, 0 FP, ±6 60 / 0 cumplida
31 a 60 literales distintos, punto 45 31 cumplida al borde, por un literal
Reparto RC 5: 240 / 55 / 8 / 3 / 2 / 0 239 / 42 / 0 / 10 / 0 / 17 dirección correcta, tres desvíos
Terceros distintos: 12 ± 6 11 cumplida

Tres desvíos que se publican porque se midieron: la imagen docker sin digest no existe en los 10 repos (predije

cuatro), y apareció una clase que no estaba en la taxonomía (R7, 17). El punto de 45 contra 31 no es un fallo de
método: es la diferencia entre estimar cuántas ocurrencias habría y contar cuántas referencias distintas hay.

7. Lo que sigue sin tasa, y por qué se dice

SC1 — 211 observaciones, y no todas son la misma cosa. No son del gate: son el recuento de sustitución y cadena
del propio arnés. Con este acto se miden 368 de 612 observaciones (60,1%) — pero ese denominador no es el de
hallazgos, y confundirlos es el defecto que este addendum ya cometió una vez con otra cifra. De las 244 sin censo,
156 son REVIEW por diseño del contrato (SC1_JOB_WRITE_SCOPE_REVIEW 153 + SC1_ROOT_READ_ALL_REVIEW 3): son

  • RC 4 3), validada por revisión de dominio con cadena, no por censo. Sobre el denominador que un CTO querría —el de las que afirman una vulnerabilidad, 456— la cobertura es 368/456 = 80,7%, y lo que falta censar son 55 casos, el 9,0% del total, no 211. title: If you're looking for what comes after wire, take a look at kanna-di
summary:
For a long time, compile-time DI in Go meant google/wire. But wire is no longer taking new features, and every so often the question comes up: what do you use instead?

This post introduces kanna-di, which I wrote to sit in that spot. Like wire, the generated code is plain Go and imports nothing at run time. The difference is that you register no providers.

What was tedious

Think about what you write for wire:

  • a wire.go with //go:build wireinject, where you declare the injector's signature yourself
  • wire.NewSet to collect providers, passed to wire.Build
  • wire.Bind for every interface
  • and every time you add a constructor, you add it to some set

In other words, telling wire which functions to use is a separate job, living somewhere other than the code. Constructors already sit next to their types. You're listing them a second time.

How kanna-di thinks about it

With kanna-di, you mark the struct that will be the container, and that's it. It looks at each field's type, finds the constructor next to that type, follows that constructor's parameters recursively, and writes a constructor that calls everything in order.

Take a layered application. The register-user use case depends on a repository for persistence and a sender for the welcome mail. Each layer keeps its constructors next to its types, as usual:

// package user, the domain
type Repository interface {
    Save(ctx context.Context, u User) error
    Find(ctx context.Context, id ID) (User, error)
}

// package mail, the domain
type Sender interface {
    Send(ctx context.Context, m Message) error
}

// package usecase
func NewRegisterUser(repo user.Repository, mailer mail.Sender) *RegisterUser
func NewGetUser(repo user.Repository) *GetUser

// package postgres, the infrastructure
func NewUserRepository(db *sql.DB) *UserRepository

// package sendgrid, an external API
func NewSender(cfg config.Config) *Sender

// package handler
func NewUser(registerUser *usecase.RegisterUser, getUser *usecase.GetUser) *User

// package config
func Load() (Config, error)

The composition root already has a struct that holds what the program is made of: the server. Mark it //kanna:container.

package main

//go:generate go tool kanna-di

//kanna:container
type server struct {
    _ user.Repository `di:"with=postgres.NewUserRepository"`
    _ mail.Sender     `di:"with=sendgrid.NewSender"`

    users *handler.User
}

func (s *server) routes() http.Handler {
    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    mux.HandleFunc("POST /users", s.users.Register)
    mux.HandleFunc("GET /users/{id}", s.users.Get)
    return mux
}

func openDB(cfg config.Config) (*sql.DB, func(), error) {
    db, err := sql.Open("pgx", cfg.DSN)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, nil, err
    }
    return db, func() { db.Close() }, nil
}

What only this root can decide is written next to it: which implementation serves each of the domain's two interfaces (with=), and how to open what the standard library provides (openDB). Nothing else.

go generate ./... writes di_gen.go:

// Code generated by kanna-di. DO NOT EDIT.

package main

import (
    "example.com/shop/internal/config"
    "example.com/shop/internal/handler"
    "example.com/shop/internal/infra/postgres"
    "example.com/shop/internal/infra/sendgrid"
    "example.com/shop/internal/usecase"
)

// newServer initializes dependencies and constructs server.
func newServer() (*server, func(), error) {
    cfg, err := config.Load()
    if err != nil {
        return nil, nil, err
    }
    db, cleanup, err := openDB(cfg)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, nil, err
    }
    repo := postgres.NewUserRepository(db)
    mailer := sendgrid.NewSender(cfg)
    registerUser := usecase.NewRegisterUser(repo, mailer)
    getUser := usecase.NewGetUser(repo)
    users := handler.NewUser(registerUser, getUser)

    return &server{
        users: users,
    }, cleanup, nil
}

*usecase.RegisterUser comes from usecase.NewRegisterUser. *sql.DB comes from openDB, next to the container. user.Repository and mail.Sender come from the implementations the container named. config.Config is loaded once and shared by openDB and sendgrid.NewSender. Nothing is registered anywhere. When a constructor's parameters change, the next go generate changes the code that calls it.

func main() {
    s, cleanup, err := newServer()
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    defer cleanup()

    log.Print(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", s.routes()))
}

How providers are found

"The function next to the type" has a precise definition. When a type is needed, kanna-di takes the first of these that has one:

  1. an argument of the constructor (di:"arg")
  2. the provider the container chose for the type (di:"with=...")
  3. an exported field of a struct the container embeds or declares as _
  4. a function in the container's own package
  5. an exported function in the package declaring the type, when that package is in your module or go.work

Finding none stops generation. So do two at the same level. A helper in a testutil package or a fixture returning the same type changes nothing unless the container names it. The standard library and other modules are never searched: io does have a function returning an io.Writer, and you would not want it picked for you.

Errors say which field

The part of DI that eats your time is when resolution fails. kanna-di's errors trace the need back to the field it started from.

The most common mistake with an interface is forgetting with=:

./server.go:12:2: error: nothing provides mail.Sender, which usecase.NewRegisterUser needs
  via server.users → handler.NewUser → usecase.NewRegisterUser
  return one from a function in package main, take it with di:"arg", or choose a provider with di:"with=..."

When there are two candidates, both positions are shown along with how to choose:

./server.go:11:2: error: 2 functions in package usecase return *usecase.GetUser
  usecase.NewGetUser (../../internal/usecase/get_user.go:12:6)
  usecase.NewCachedGetUser (../../internal/usecase/get_user.go:30:6)
  via server.users → handler.NewUser
  choose one with _ *usecase.GetUser `di:"with=usecase.NewGetUser"`

Typos get a did you mean, and if the implementation chosen with with= does not satisfy the interface, the error names the missing method.

Taking a container apart in tests

This is where I think the difference from wire is largest.

In tests you want the repository swapped for an in-memory one and the mail sender for something that only records. With wire, that means another injector and another set. With kanna-di, you declare a container in a _test.go file and embed the production server.

//kanna:container
type testServer struct {
    *server

    _ user.Repository `di:"arg"`
    _ mail.Sender     `di:"arg"`
}

func TestRegisterUser(t *testing.T) {
    sent := &mailtest.Recorder{}
    s := newTestServer(memory.NewUserRepository(), sent)
    srv := httptest.NewServer(s.routes())
    defer srv.Close()

    // POST /users ...

    if len(sent.Messages) != 1 {
        t.Fatalf("want 1 welcome mail, got %d", len(sent.Messages))
    }
}

Embedding a container from the same package rebuilds it here, field by field. Because the two interfaces are now declared as arguments, the with= bindings are unused, and nothing needs *sql.DB or config.Config anymore. So openDB, config.Load, and sendgrid.NewSender are never called, and newTestServer returns neither a cleanup nor an error. In production the root chooses the implementations; in tests you pass them in. That's all.

The output goes to di_gen_test.go. The chicken-and-egg problem, where the test calls newTestServer before it has been generated, is handled by kanna-di: it type-checks once more with what it is about to write in place, so a call to a not-yet-generated constructor does not stop it.

In a real application

showcase is a gRPC todo service that uses kanna-di across its layers:

  • internal/di holds the Config and Infra containers; NewInfra assembles the pgx pool and the transactor
  • each operation in usecase is a container of its own; NewPutTodo and NewDeleteTodo are generated
  • the handler container bundles the use cases into NewHandler

A use case looks like this:

//kanna:container
type DeleteTodo struct {
    _ *infra.Deps // infra.NewDeps provides it; its Transactor and Todos fill the fields below

    transactor tx.Transactor
    todos      repository.Todo
}

A struct in a _ field is not stored; it only serves the container. The use case takes exactly what it needs from what the infrastructure bundled.

A struct with no fields, such as the todov1.UnimplementedTodoServiceServer a gRPC handler embeds, is left at its zero value. No provider is needed for it.

Cleanup

Providers returning T, func() or T, func(), error have their cleanups collected into one. They run in reverse order, and when a provider fails, the cleanups of those that ran before it are called before the error is returned. Same behavior as wire. Anything taken as an argument or drawn from an embedded struct belongs to the caller and is never closed.

The honest part

  • Requires Go 1.26. It is designed to be installed with go get -tool
  • It is v0, written by one person, and the API still moves
  • A generic struct cannot be a container: there is no way to choose its type arguments
  • Within one directory, test containers can live in either the in-package test package or the external _test package, not both
  • Rule 5 (searching the type's own package) only covers your module and go.work. Constructors in dependencies are never picked up automatically. This is deliberate

kanna-di is one of the kanna family of generators, but it stands on its own. It shares nothing with the other tools, and the generated code calls only your functions.

Try it 

go get -tool github.com/go-kanna/di/cmd/kanna-di

Mark the struct with //kanna:container, add //go:generate go tool kanna-di, run go generate ./....

If you're coming from wire: the functions you listed in wire.NewSet are most likely already next to their types, so they're found as they are. What you bound with wire.Bind becomes a field on the container that names the provider directly:

_ user.Repository `di:"with=postgres.NewUserRepository"`

What used to live in two places, the Bind and the Set, is this one line. And you no longer write the injector's signature; it follows from the container struct.

The repository has an example/ directory with the layout from this post, runnable as is.

Disclosure: kanna-di is a rewrite of mickamy/injector, an earlier tool of mine. The idea is the same: a container struct, and constructors found next to their types. The inject tag became di, the directive became //kanna:container, and embedded test containers and cleanup handling were added. injector is archived; development continues here.

// Code generated by kanna-di. DO NOT EDIT.

package main

import (
    "example.com/shop/internal/config"
    "example.com/shop/internal/handler"
    "example.com/shop/internal/infra/postgres"
    "example.com/shop/internal/infra/sendgrid"
    "example.com/shop/internal/usecase"
)

// newServer initializes dependencies and constructs server.
func newServer() (*server, func(), error) {
    cfg, err := config.Load()
    if err != nil {
        return nil, nil, err
    }
    db, cleanup, err := openDB(cfg)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, nil, err
    }
    repo := postgres.NewUserRepository(db)
    mailer := sendgrid.NewSender(cfg)
    registerUser := usecase.NewRegisterUser(repo, mailer)
    getUser := usecase.NewGetUser(repo)
    users := handler.NewUser(registerUser, getUser)

    return &server{
        users: users,
    }, cleanup, nil
}

*usecase.RegisterUser comes from usecase.NewRegisterUser. *sql.DB comes from openDB, next to the container. user.Repository and mail.Sender come from the implementations the container named. config.Config is loaded once and shared by openDB and sendgrid.NewSender. Nothing is registered anywhere. When a constructor's parameters change, the next go generate changes the code that calls it.

func main() {
    s, cleanup, err := newServer()
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    defer cleanup()

    log.Print(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", s.routes()))
}

How providers are found

"The function next to the type" has a precise definition. When a type is needed, kanna-di takes the first of these that has one:

  1. an argument of the constructor (di:"arg")
  2. the provider the container chose for the type (di:"with=...")
  3. an exported field of a struct the container embeds or declares as _
  4. a function in the container's own package
  5. an exported function in the package declaring the type, when that package is in your module or go.work

Finding none stops generation. So do two at the same level. A helper in a testutil package or a fixture returning the same type changes nothing unless the container names it. The standard library and other modules are never searched: io does have a function returning an io.Writer, and you would not want it picked for you.

Errors say which field

The part of DI that eats your time is when resolution fails. kanna-di's errors trace the need back to the field it started from.

The most common mistake with an interface is forgetting with=:

./server.go:12:2: error: nothing provides mail.Sender, which usecase.NewRegisterUser needs
  via server.users → handler.NewUser → usecase.NewRegisterUser
  return one from a function in package main, take it with di:"arg", or choose a provider with di:"with=..."

When there are two candidates, both positions are shown along with how to choose:

./server.go:11:2: error: 2 functions in package usecase return *usecase.GetUser
  usecase.NewGetUser (../../internal/usecase/get_user.go:12:6)
  usecase.NewCachedGetUser (../../internal/usecase/get_user.go:30:6)
  via server.users → handler.NewUser
  choose one with _ *usecase.GetUser `di:"with=usecase.NewGetUser"`

Typos get a did you mean, and if the implementation chosen with with= does not satisfy the interface, the error names the missing method.

Taking a container apart in tests

This is where I think the difference from wire is largest.

In tests you want the repository swapped for an in-memory one and the mail sender for something that only records. With wire, that means another injector and another set. With kanna-di, you declare a container in a _test.go file and embed the production server.

//kanna:container
type testServer struct {
    *server

    _ user.Repository `di:"arg"`
    _ mail.Sender     `di:"arg"`
}

func TestRegisterUser(t *testing.T) {
    sent := &mailtest.Recorder{}
    s := newTestServer(memory.NewUserRepository(), sent)
    srv := httptest.NewServer(s.routes())
    defer srv.Close()

    // POST /users ...

    if len(sent.Messages) != 1 {
        t.Fatalf("want 1 welcome mail, got %d", len(sent.Messages))
    }
}

Embedding a container from the same package rebuilds it here, field by field. Because the two interfaces are now declared as arguments, the with= bindings are unused, and nothing needs *sql.DB or config.Config anymore. So openDB, config.Load, and sendgrid.NewSender are never called, and newTestServer returns neither a cleanup nor an error. In production the root chooses the implementations; in tests you pass them in. That's all.

The output goes to di_gen_test.go. The chicken-and-egg problem, where the test calls newTestServer before it has been generated, is handled by kanna-di: it type-checks once more with what it is about to write in place, so a call to a not-yet-generated constructor does not stop it.

In a real application

showcase is a gRPC todo service that uses kanna-di across its layers:

  • internal/di holds the Config and Infra containers; NewInfra assembles the pgx pool and the transactor
  • each operation in usecase is a container of its own; NewPutTodo and NewDeleteTodo are generated
  • the handler container bundles the use cases into NewHandler

A use case looks like this:

//kanna:container
type DeleteTodo struct {
    _ *infra.Deps // infra.NewDeps provides it; its Transactor and Todos fill the fields below

    transactor tx.Transactor
    todos      repository.Todo
}

A struct in a _ field is not stored; it only serves the container. The use case takes exactly what it needs from what the infrastructure bundled.

A struct with no fields, such as the todov1.UnimplementedTodoServiceServer a gRPC handler embeds, is left at its zero value. No provider is needed for it.

Cleanup

Providers returning T, func() or T, func(), error have their cleanups collected into one. They run in reverse order, and when a provider fails, the cleanups of those that ran before it are called before the error is returned. Same behavior as wire. Anything taken as an argument or drawn from an embedded struct belongs to the caller and is never closed.

The honest part

  • Requires Go 1.26. It is designed to be installed with go get -tool
  • It is v0, written by one person, and the API still moves
  • A generic struct cannot be a container: there is no way to choose its type arguments
  • Within one directory, test containers can live in either the in-package test package or the external _test package, not both
  • Rule 5 (searching the type's own package) only covers your module and go.work. Constructors in dependencies are never picked up automatically. This is deliberate

kanna-di is one of the kanna family of generators, but it stands on its own. It shares nothing with the other tools, and the generated code calls only your functions.

Try it 

go get -tool github.com/go-kanna/di/cmd/kanna-di

Mark the struct with //kanna:container, add //go:generate go tool kanna-di, run go generate ./....

If you're coming from wire: the functions you listed in wire.NewSet are most likely already next to their types, so they're found as they are. What you bound with wire.Bind becomes a field on the container that names the provider directly:

_ user.Repository `di:"with=postgres.NewUserRepository"`

What used to live in two places, the Bind and the Set, is this one line. And you no longer write the injector's signature; it follows from the container struct.

The repository has an example/ directory with the layout from this post, runnable as is.

Disclosure: kanna-di is a rewrite of mickamy/injector, an earlier tool of mine. The idea is the same: a container struct, and constructors found next to their types. The inject tag became di, the directive became //kanna:container, and embedded test containers and cleanup handling were added. injector is archived; development continues here.

title: How I built an asynchronous predictive compiler using Git Worktrees and Docker
summary:
Current AI coding tools have a fundamental workflow problem: they are entirely reactive.

You write a function, you run your test suite, it fails, you copy the error logs, paste them into the AI chat, and wait for a fix. You are the orchestrator, and the AI is just glorified autocomplete.

I wanted an engine that operates entirely in the gap between keystrokes. I wanted a system that detects my unfinished code, spins up a parallel replica of my project, tests it, and patches the broken dependencies before I even hit git commit.

So, I built Shadow-Branch Engine. It is a background daemon that uses Git hardlinks, AST pruning, and zero-trust Docker sandboxing to test and heal your code asynchronously.

Here is how the architecture works under the hood.

  1. Bypassing the npm install Bottleneck The biggest challenge of running background tests is environment replication. If I want to test uncommitted changes in the background, I can't just copy the directory—running npm install on a massive node_modules folder takes way too long.

To solve this, Shadow-Branch manipulates the filesystem directly. When you save a file, the daemon triggers a git stash create and instantly mounts a hidden parallel git worktree. It uses OS-level hardlinks to mirror your existing node_modules.

The result? A sub-millisecond, fully isolated replica of your codebase, ready for execution.

  1. AST Token Pruning (ts-morph) Passing an entire codebase into an LLM context window to generate tests is incredibly expensive and slow.

Instead of dumping raw text, Shadow-Branch uses the TypeScript Compiler API (ts-morph). When a file is saved, the engine parses the Abstract Syntax Tree (AST), identifies the specific function you modified, and traces its exact dependency graph.

It strips away all unrelated files and comments, sending only the mathematically necessary context to the local AI. This drops the token count by over 90%, making local model execution incredibly fast.

  1. The Docker Execution Sandbox Once the AI generates the test suite or a patch, we cannot just run it directly on the host machine. AI-generated code is inherently untrusted.

Shadow-Branch uses the dockerode library to dynamically spin up a lightweight, network-isolated Docker container mapped only to the .shadow-workspace. It executes the test suite inside the container.

If the test fails, the daemon captures the exit codes and routes the error logs back through a local XState state machine for an autonomous healing loop. If the test passes, it surfaces a clean, ready-to-merge patch directly to your IDE.

  1. Parallel Fuzzing Swarms Because the engine runs asynchronously, it has the luxury of time that a blocking terminal command does not.

If the AST detects asynchronous operations (Promise.all, database transactions), Shadow-Branch doesn't just run one test. It spins up a swarm of 10 parallel Micro-VMs inside Docker to aggressively fuzz for race conditions. If even one container fails, the patch is rejected.

The Code
I just open-sourced the entire Shadow-Branch Engine today. It is built strictly as a local Node.js daemon with zero dependencies on external, closed-source SaaS platforms.

If you are interested in Git manipulation, AST parsing, or local Docker orchestration, check out the repository. We have several open issues tagged help wanted for adding Python and Rust LSP support.

Repository: https://github.com/hariom123-dev/Shadow-Branch.git

Let me know your thoughts on the architecture in the comments. I'd love to hear how other people are handling local autonomous execution!

title: A ghost moved into my terminal. It runs on Gemma, and it never leaves my laptop
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

The first time I ran it for real, Gemma said nothing at all. Eight commands, eight empty lines. The ghost was there, it just wouldn't speak. That turned out to be the most honest bug I've ever hit in a Halloween project, and I'll get to it.

What I Built

haunted-terminal is a ghost that moves into your zsh, and it doesn't just leave comments. It haunts the place.

When you open a terminal:

  1. The ghost rises. A full-screen ASCII ghost fades in out of the dark, bobs, blinks, and fades away.
  2. The music starts. A horror soundtrack loops for as long as any haunted tab is open, and stops when you close the last one.
  3. The welcome card appears. The same ghost floats beside your status (is Gemma awake, is the music on, where you are) until you press a key.
  4. Then it stays. About one command in three, it whispers a line about what you just did. Every few commands, something in the room makes a sound: a whispered boo right behind your ear, a wolf, a witch cackling, chains on stone.

The ghost is a programmer who died in 1987 at a VT100 terminal, halfway through a COBOL migration. He is cold, a little jealous of the living, and he never gives advice.

He also has one job that is not a joke. Before you press Enter on rm -rf, git push --force, git reset --hard, DROP TABLE or curl ... | sh, he stops you and asks if you're sure.

And on November 1 and 2, for Día de los Muertos, the welcome card turns marigold, and the ghost builds a small ofrenda for everything you deleted that day.

The ghost is Gemma 4 E2B, running on my laptop through llama.cpp. Nothing I type goes to a server.

Demo

A two-minute tour: the ghost rising, the welcome card, real Gemma whispers on git status, npm test and a typo, a wolf howl from the ElevenLabs sounds, the rm -rf guard, the Día de los Muertos card, and how to install it. Turn the sound on.

Every ghost line in that picture is real Gemma output. A few more from the test runs:

$ git log --oneline -5
  👻 Five commits remain, the ghosts of my forgotten logic.
$ git checkout feature/login        (exit 128)
  👻 The branch is gone, just like my last memory of warmth.
$ git status
  👻 The changes remain, just like the dust on this old screen.
$ npm test                           (exit 1)
  👻 That error is familiar; the same ghost in the machine.

Website: haunted-terminal-lovat.vercel.app, with the same ghost animated in your browser and a button to play the soundtrack.

The ghost is Gemma 4, running on your own machine through llama.cpp. Your shell history never leaves your laptop.

Every ghost line above is real Gemma output from a laptop, about half a second each.

Hacktoberfest 2026 · Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

This is my entry for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 4: Ghost in the Machine. The week asks for a spooky build with open-source AI at its core. Here the ghost is the open model: Gemma 4, running on your own laptop, gives the…

View on GitHub

Two files do the work, with no dependencies beyond Python's standard library: ghost.zsh (the hooks) and ghost (everything else).

How I Built It

The architecture is small. ghost.zsh hooks into zsh in two places. After every command, precmd hands the command and its exit code to the ghost. Before Enter, a wrapped accept-line widget runs the safety check. When a terminal opens, it starts the music and plays the intro. The ghost script talks to llama-server's OpenAI-compatible endpoint, draws the animations, and manages the sound.

Most of what I learned came from things going wrong.

1. The ghost that wouldn't speak

That first live run: eight commands, eight empty replies. The raw response showed why. Gemma 4 starts thinking as soon as it gets a system prompt, and it spent all 60 of its tokens reasoning about how to be a ghost:

"content": "",
"reasoning_content": "Thinking Process:\n\n1. **Analyze the Request & Persona:**..."

One flag fixed it: "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false}. A ghost should blurt, not deliberate. There's now a test so this can't quietly come back.

2. "Another…"

Once it spoke, it started a lot of lines the same way: Another triumph. Another failure. Another branch lost. So I measured it. I wrote eval_ghost.py, which runs 40 everyday commands (git, npm, docker, typos, failed builds) through the ghost three times and checks every reply.

Then I added four example replies to the prompt, told it to notice one concrete detail of the command, and skipped commands like ls and cd that aren't worth a ghost's breath. Here's the before and after, 120 replies each:

Check Before After
Replied at all 100% 100%
Under 20 words 100% 100%
Gave no advice 100% 100%
No emoji, quotes or hashtags 100% 100%
Didn't open with "Another" 82% 97%
One sentence 82% 88%
Median reply time 0.7 s 0.7 s

Most of the remaining "two sentence" replies are fragments like "Five commits. Such a brief, pathetic life for code.", which honestly suit him. The examples cost no speed: llama-server caches the shared prompt, so old and new run at the same median.

3. The safety check is not the model

A warning before rm -rf has to be instant and right every time, so it's plain pattern matching. Gemma only does the part where being creative is the point. The same script tests it:

Safety check Result
Dangerous commands caught 19/19
Harmless look-alikes left alone 19/19 (was 17/19)

The two false alarms were grep -r 'DROP TABLE' migrations and echo 'drop table' > notes.txt. Now DROP only counts inside a database client like psql or mysql.

4. Secrets never reach the model

Even a local model shouldn't see your keys, and the ghost could repeat one on screen. Before a command reaches Gemma, anything that looks like a secret is blanked: export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-..., --password=..., Bearer tokens, https://user:token@..., and GitHub, Slack and AWS key formats. npm test stays npm test. echo $GITHUB_TOKEN stays too, because a variable name isn't a secret.

5. A voice that talked too much

My first version had ElevenLabs read every ghost line aloud. It was too much within a minute. A ghost that talks constantly isn't scary. A sound you didn't expect is.

So now the shell keeps a counter. After every one to three commands (two on average, which I checked over 30 commands), it plays one of seven horror sounds made with the ElevenLabs sound effects API: a breathy boo, a wolf howl, a witch's cackle, a creaking door, a moan, dragging chains, overlapping whispers. Each is generated once and cached. After that they cost no credits, work offline, and ElevenLabs never sees a single command.

6. Colours that didn't exist

The welcome card's title came out garbled on my Mac, with some letters invisible. macOS Terminal.app can't display 24-bit colour, and I had used it for a gradient. The card now uses only the 256-colour palette, with a solid white title and a violet base.

The rest

  • The ghost is a signed distance field: a circle for the head and a box with a wavy hem for the body, drawn in @$% and lit by a violet and green halo. The website draws its hero with the same math in JavaScript.
  • The welcome card redraws in place 20 times a second until you press a key, and that key isn't typed into your prompt.
  • One music player serves every tab. An atomic lock file stops two tabs from starting two players. (They did, the first time. Testing caught it.) Each shell registers itself, and the music stops when none are left.
  • No server, no ghost. If llama-server is down, the ghost stays silent in milliseconds. It never blocks the shell.
  • Tests: 15 unit tests, plus an interactive zsh test that drives a real shell through a pseudo-terminal. It types rm -rf, presses n, and checks the folder survived. GitHub Actions runs them on every push.

I built this with Claude Code as my pair programmer.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A terminal sees everything: file paths, hostnames, branch names, half-typed secrets, the command you ran at 2 a.m. I would never pipe that into a hosted API to get a joke back.

With an open-weight model I don't have to. Gemma runs on my machine, so:

  • It works offline. On a plane, in a basement, with Wi-Fi off.
  • My shell history stays mine. No account, no logs on someone else's server.
  • It costs nothing to run. A ghost that comments hundreds of times a day would be a real bill on a paid API. Here it's zero.
  • No lock-in. GHOST_URL points at any OpenAI-compatible server. Swapping Gemma for another open model is one flag to llama-server.

This only works because open models are now small and good enough to sit next to your shell and answer in under a second. A year ago this would have been a cloud API with a privacy policy. Now it's a file on my disk.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma: Gemma 4 E2B is the ghost, running locally through llama.cpp, with thinking turned off, example-driven prompting, and a measured before and after.
  • Best Use of ElevenLabs: seven horror sound effects made with the ElevenLabs sound effects API, played at random every one to three commands and cached so they work offline.
  • Best Use of GitHub Copilot: GitHub Actions runs the unit tests and a zsh syntax check on every push.

Music: "Horror Music" by kiravale, via Pixabay. Code: MIT. Demo video: built with the onetake motion skill (PolyForm Noncommercial), narrated with the open Kokoro TTS model. The terminal in it is redrawn from the ghost's own code, and every ghost line in it is real Gemma output.
