Dangerous commands caught 19/19
Harmless look-alikes left alone 19/19 (was 17/19)

The two false alarms were grep -r 'DROP TABLE' migrations and echo 'drop table' > notes.txt. Now DROP only counts inside a database client like psql or mysql.

4. Secrets never reach the model

Even a local model shouldn't see your keys, and the ghost could repeat one on screen. Before a command reaches Gemma, anything that looks like a secret is blanked: export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-..., --password=..., Bearer tokens, https://user:token@..., and GitHub, Slack and AWS key formats. npm test stays npm test. echo $GITHUB_TOKEN stays too, because a variable name isn't a secret.

5. A voice that talked too much

My first version had ElevenLabs read every ghost line aloud. It was too much within a minute. A ghost that talks constantly isn't scary. A sound you didn't expect is.

So now the shell keeps a counter. After every one to three commands (two on average, which I checked over 30 commands), it plays one of seven horror sounds made with the ElevenLabs sound effects API: a breathy boo, a wolf howl, a witch's cackle, a creaking door, a moan, dragging chains, overlapping whispers. Each is generated once and cached. After that they cost no credits, work offline, and ElevenLabs never sees a single command.

6. Colours that didn't exist

The welcome card's title came out garbled on my Mac, with some letters invisible. macOS Terminal.app can't display 24-bit colour, and I had used it for a gradient. The card now uses only the 256-colour palette, with a solid white title and a violet base.

The rest

  • The ghost is a signed distance field: a circle for the head and a box with a wavy hem for the body, drawn in @$% and lit by a violet and green halo. The website draws its hero with the same math in JavaScript.
  • The welcome card redraws in place 20 times a second until you press a key, and that key isn't typed into your prompt.
  • One music player serves every tab. An atomic lock file stops two tabs from starting two players. (They did, the first time. Testing caught it.) Each shell registers itself, and the music stops when none are left.
  • No server, no ghost. If llama-server is down, the ghost stays silent in milliseconds. It never blocks the shell.
  • Tests: 15 unit tests, plus an interactive zsh test that drives a real shell through a pseudo-terminal. It types rm -rf, presses n, and checks the folder survived. GitHub Actions runs them on every push.

I built this with Claude Code as my pair programmer.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A terminal sees everything: file paths, hostnames, branch names, half-typed secrets, the command you ran at 2 a.m. I would never pipe that into a hosted API to get a joke back.

With an open-weight model I don't have to. Gemma runs on my machine, so:

  • It works offline. On a plane, in a basement, with Wi-Fi off.
  • My shell history stays mine. No account, no logs on someone else's server.
  • It costs nothing to run. A ghost that comments hundreds of times a day would be a real bill on a paid API. Here it's zero.
  • No lock-in. GHOST_URL points at any OpenAI-compatible server. Swapping Gemma for another open model is one flag to llama-server.

This only works because open models are now small and good enough to sit next to your shell and answer in under a second. A year ago this would have been a cloud API with a privacy policy. Now it's a file on my disk.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma: Gemma 4 E2B is the ghost, running locally through llama.cpp, with thinking turned off, example-driven prompting, and a measured before and after.
  • Best Use of ElevenLabs: seven horror sound effects made with the ElevenLabs sound effects API, played at random every one to three commands and cached so they work offline.
  • Best Use of GitHub Copilot: GitHub Actions runs the unit tests and a zsh syntax check on every push.

Music: "Horror Music" by kiravale, via Pixabay. Code: MIT. Demo video: built with the onetake motion skill (PolyForm Noncommercial), narrated with the open Kokoro TTS model. The terminal in it is redrawn from the ghost's own code, and every ghost line in it is real Gemma output.

title: I Built RepoGeist: An Open-Source AI That Uncovers the Ghosts in Your Git History
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

There is code in your repository that nobody can see anymore.

It had a filename. Someone spent an afternoon writing it. Another developer changed it three weeks later. Then one commit removed it, the branch moved on, and the reason slowly disappeared from the team's memory.

Git remembers the code. It does not explain the story.

What I Built

RepoGeist is a privacy-first Git archaeology application that reconstructs a repository's past and lets you investigate it with a local open-weight AI model.

The deterministic half reads real Git objects. It counts commits and contributors, traces file activity, identifies quiet branches, finds files deleted from the analyzed HEAD, and retrieves their last historical versions without modifying the working tree.

The generative half turns selected evidence into explanations. Ghost Chat answers questions about the repository. Commit Autopsy interprets a bounded diff. The Repository Speaks transforms factual milestones into a haunted chronicle, technical documentary, or developer retrospective. Answers include references to the commits and files supplied as evidence.

My interpretation of “Ghost in the Machine” is both literal and practical: the ghosts are deleted modules, abandoned experiments, and decisions whose authors are no longer in the room.

Demo

Demo video: Watch on YouTube

The most revealing route through RepoGeist's synthetic demo repository is:

  1. RepoGeist analyzes ten deterministic commits and a stale experiment branch.
  2. The Graveyard reveals auth/legacy.py, which no longer exists at HEAD.
  3. Code Resurrection displays its final historical version directly from Git.
  4. Ghost Chat receives the deletion commit, related authentication changes, and bounded metadata.
  5. The answer explains what the evidence proves. If Git never documents why it happened, RepoGeist says the motivation is unknown.

That last constraint matters. A confident ghost that invents history is just a hallucination wearing a costume.

Code

AryanSharma9917 / repogeist

👻 RepoGeist

Every repository has a past. Some commits still haunt it.

RepoGeist is a privacy-first Git archaeology platform. It reconstructs real repository history, finds code absent from HEAD, surfaces quiet branches, retrieves historical source, and lets a local open-weight model explain the evidence without sending source code to a third party.

Built for the Hacktoberfest 2026 Open-Source AI Challenge — Week 4, Ghost in the Machine.

What works

  • Secure import beneath one configured repository root
  • Deterministic commit, contributor, file, language, activity, and branch analysis
  • Deleted-file detection and read-only historical content retrieval
  • Searchable timeline, repository graveyard, and responsive Spectral Terminal UI
  • Evidence retrieval and locally hosted Ollama chat with commit/file citations
  • Bounded-diff commit autopsies and three evidence-grounded story styles
  • Markdown and JSON investigation reports
  • Analysis jobs with real stage-based progress
  • Reproducible ten-commit synthetic demo plus stale experiment branch
  • Docker Compose, API tests, typechecking, production build, and CI

The…

View on GitHub

Repository: github.com/AryanSharma9917/repogeist

The repository includes Docker Compose, a reproducible demo-repository generator, FastAPI OpenAPI documentation, architecture and security guides, automated tests, and CI that does not require downloading model weights.

How I Built It

The frontend is built with Next.js and TypeScript. The backend uses FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, and SQLite. RepoGeist invokes native Git using argument arrays with hooks disabled; it never executes code from an analyzed repository. A configured repository-root boundary prevents the API from browsing arbitrary paths on the host.

The core architectural decision was to keep Git facts separate from AI prose:

Git repository
  -> deterministic extraction
  -> SQLite evidence records
  -> bounded keyword/entity retrieval
  -> local Ollama prompt
  -> evidence-linked response

RepoGeist uses the open-weight Qwen2.5 3B model through Ollama by default. Both the runtime URL and model name are configurable. The model never receives the entire repository; it sees a bounded evidence packet containing relevant commit metadata, changed paths, deletion records, and, for a commit autopsy, a limited diff.

Repository content is treated as untrusted data. A commit message could contain prompt-injection text, so the system prompt explicitly says that repository-derived text is evidence, not instructions. The model receives no tools for shell execution, arbitrary file access, secret access, repository mutation, or outbound requests.

The application remains useful without Ollama. If local AI is unavailable, only the AI endpoints return setup guidance. The factual dashboard, timeline, Graveyard, Code Resurrection, and deterministic reports still work.

What I verified

  • Six backend tests pass against real temporary Git repositories.
  • Ruff linting and TypeScript checking pass.
  • The Next.js production build succeeds and generates eleven application routes.
  • Docker Compose configuration and the frontend/backend Docker builds succeed.
  • The backend container completed a real demo import, ten-commit analysis, Graveyard lookup, and historical-source retrieval.
  • The installed frontend dependency tree reports zero known vulnerabilities.
  • A real Ollama run with qwen2.5:3b produced a Ghost Chat answer citing the authentication deletion commit and auth/legacy.py while correctly acknowledging that the exact motivation was undocumented.
  • A real Haunted Chronicle returned chronological inline citations and a complete evidence panel.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Repository history can contain unreleased features, internal names, security fixes, and architectural clues. Sending all of it to a closed hosted API by default would be the wrong privacy model.

Local inference changes the product, not just its cost. Source code, Git history, prompts, and model responses can remain on the developer's machine. RepoGeist works without an AI subscription, and a team can swap models, inspect the grounding prompt, adjust retrieval, or work completely offline. The deterministic analyzer is open to inspection, so users can distinguish facts extracted from Git from interpretations generated by the model.

Open-weight is not automatically the same as unrestricted open source, and every model's license still deserves review. However, the ability to possess and run the weights locally is what makes RepoGeist's privacy promise technically credible.

The Spirit of It

The moment I want the demo to land is not the animated title. It is a small sentence beneath a polished AI answer:

The file was removed in this commit, but the repository does not document the developer's exact motivation.

That admission is the heart of RepoGeist. Git archaeology is not necromancy. We can recover evidence, preserve context, and tell a compelling story, but we should not put words in the mouths of developers who are not there to correct us.

Sometimes respecting the dead means letting the record end where it ends.

title: Cuéntame: a local Gemma interviewer that preserves the words you actually said
summary:
What I Built

In Panama, the Day of the Dead on November 2 can mean visiting a grave, cleaning it, and remembering someone through ordinary details: a Sunday meal, a phrase they repeated, the sound of a familiar place. I wanted a tool for collecting those details while the people who know them can still tell the story.

Cuéntame is a small command-line interview. Gemma runs locally through Ollama and asks one question at a time about a person you want to remember. The program saves the answers as a Markdown page. The model is allowed to ask; it is not allowed to write the person's life story. The saved page is assembled by Python from the exact answers entered by the storyteller.

My interpretation of Ghost in the Machine is a question that helps a living person remember, without pretending to be the person who is gone.

Demo

The repository has a clearly fictional formatting example:

python3 cuentame.py --ejemplo

That command does not call a model. For the actual interview, run Ollama with gemma4:e2b, then:

python3 cuentame.py --nombre "Elena" --modelo gemma4:e2b

Gemma proposes each next question using the earlier questions and answers. A fictional answer such as “Hacía arroz con coco los domingos” goes into the file verbatim. If you never answer who taught Elena to cook, the file does not claim to know.

I ran this short end-to-end check with the locally installed gemma4:e2b model and a fictional answer:

$ python3 cuentame.py --nombre 'Elena (ficticia)' --preguntas 1
¿Cuál es un recuerdo de comida que te gustaría compartir sobre Elena?
> Hacía arroz con coco los domingos.
Guardado en recuerdos/recuerdo-elena-ficticia.md

The resulting page contains the prompt and the original answer:

## 1. ¿Cuál es un recuerdo de comida que te gustaría compartir sobre Elena?

> Hacía arroz con coco los domingos.

The output lives under recuerdos/, which is excluded from Git. The CLI refuses to overwrite an existing memory. The public examples contain fictional answers only.

Code

yosef7 / cuentame

Local family-memory interview with Gemma and Ollama

Cuéntame

Una pequeña entrevistadora local para conservar recuerdos familiares sin pedirle a la IA que invente una biografía. Gemma, mediante Ollama en 127.0.0.1, propone una pregunta a la vez. El archivo final copia literalmente las respuestas de la persona entrevistada. Los vacíos quedan abiertos.

Proyecto creado para Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 4, tema Ghost in the Machine. La demo ficticia y las pruebas de código no equivalen a una ejecución real del modelo.

Uso

Requiere Python 3.10+ y Ollama. Descarga un modelo Gemma compatible con tu equipo y usa su nombre exacto con --modelo. El valor predeterminado es gemma4:e2b.

ollama pull gemma4:e2b
python3 cuentame.py --nombre "Elena" --modelo gemma4:e2b

Para ver solo el formato de salida, sin modelo:

python3 cuentame.py --ejemplo

Los resultados van a recuerdos/, excluido de Git. El programa no sobrescribe archivos existentes. El ejemplo usa una persona y…

View on GitHub

The project uses Python's standard library, the local Ollama /api/generate endpoint, and an open-weight Gemma model. It is MIT licensed. The README explains installation and testing; no cloud account or API key is needed.

How I Built It

The boundary is intentionally narrow:

Storyteller's answers
       |              previous Q&A
       |                  |
       |                  v
       |           local Gemma -> next question
       v
Python copies exact answers -> private Markdown file

ask_question() sends the interview history only to 127.0.0.1:11434. The prompt asks for one short, open question and forbids fabricated facts or impersonation. The program rejects empty, multiline, overlong, or non-question replies. The model response is displayed as a question; it is never used as a memory answer.

render_memory() writes the storyteller's responses as block quotes. It does not ask Gemma for a summary. That is a deliberate technical choice: a fluent summary can introduce a detail nobody said. A source-grounded keepsake is more useful than a beautiful invented biography.

The first live run revealed a practical Gemma 4 issue: with a short output limit, the model spent its tokens in its internal thinking field and returned no visible question. Setting think: false in the Ollama request produced a short question. There are three focused tests for the local request, history passed to the model, invalid model output, and literal preservation of an answer. I also completed the one-question live check above. A full family interview remains untested and should be reviewed by the storyteller.

Why Open Innovation Matters

Family recollections are private. An open-weight model running on the same laptop lets the interview continue without sending those answers to a hosted model. Markdown is a portable output: a family can read it years later without the original app or a subscription. Python and Ollama are replaceable pieces rather than a service that must remain online.

This does not prove a memory is historically accurate. The storyteller may misremember, and Gemma may ask a poor or leading question. The person using the tool should skip a question that feels wrong and review the file before sharing it. What the program can guarantee is narrower and testable: it does not turn generated prose into an attributed family fact.

Prize Category

I used Gemma as the local question generator, so this project also fits Best Use of Gemma. The same core is needed for the general Week 4 theme; no other partner service is claimed.

Prepared with AI assistance. The author approved publication.

title: Giving an AI assistant a memory of your Google search traffic that does not go stale
summary:
Picture this.

You ask your AI assistant which pages bring in the most search traffic. It answers with confidence. The numbers are from three months ago, for a site you stopped managing in August.

Nothing crashed. The assistant just kept a memory of data that is no longer true.

I wanted a memory of Google search traffic that stays current, and that forgets what it should. So for Mergetober I built a Google Search Console connector for Cognee. The code lives in PR #584 for issue #4793.

What it does

Cognee turns documents into a knowledge graph that an agent can search. The connector feeds it from Search Console. You sign in with Google, pick your properties, and it syncs how they perform in search.

Search Console gives you numbers, not prose. One row per date, query and page would be millions of documents, and an LLM would read every one. So the connector groups the data by calendar month. Each month of a property becomes:

  • an overview: totals, devices, top countries, top queries and top pages;
  • one document per top page, with the queries that led to it.

All of a property's documents share one node set. The same query in two months becomes one entity in the graph, so you can ask how it changed.

source = google_search_console_source(
    sites=["sc-domain:example.com"],  # leave it out for every verified property
    months=3,
)
await cognee.remember(source, dataset_name="search_console",
                      primary_key="id", write_disposition="merge")

Sign-in is OAuth 2.0 with the read-only scope. Run login.py once, in the browser, and the token is cached in a private file.

Data that is late and sampled

Two things make Search Console different from a normal source.

First, the newest data is late and preliminary. Google publishes final numbers about two days behind, and it can still revise the last days. So the connector reads final data only. A month stays open until it is a few days older than that lag. An open month is read again on every run. Then it is read one last time and closed, and a closed month is never read again. Only documents whose text changed are sent on, so an unchanged run makes no LLM call.

Second, the data is sampled. Google returns the top rows by clicks and leaves out rare queries for privacy. That means a query that disappears from a response is not a deleted query, and the rows never add up to the totals. Every document says so.

What gets forgotten

A property you remove, deselect, or lose verification on is forgotten whole, with its documents. I added a few safety rules, because a wrong delete is worse than a missed one:

  • A failed request never deletes anything. The run stops and the next one starts from the same spot.

run 2  {'sites': 1, 'periods': 1, 'closed': 2, 'documents': 0, ...}

That empty property showed me something my fake got wrong.

    sites=["sc-domain:example.com"],  # leave it out for every verified property
    months=3,
)
